summary: Dynamic memory allocation lets a program request heap memory at run time, sized by data it only learns while running. C provides four functions in <stdlib.h>: malloc, calloc, realloc, and free. You must check every request and release every block exactly once.

sections.heading: malloc
sections.body: `void *malloc(size_t size)` returns a pointer to `size` uninitialized bytes, or NULL on failure. The idiom `sizeof *p` keeps the size correct if the type changes.
sections.code:
int *p = malloc(10 * sizeof *p);
if (p == NULL) { perror("malloc"); return 1; }

sections.heading: calloc
sections.body: `void *calloc(size_t n, size_t size)` allocates n elements and sets all bytes to zero. It also detects overflow in n * size, which a hand-written multiplication for malloc would not.

sections.heading: realloc
sections.body: `void *realloc(void *p, size_t new_size)` resizes a block, preserving contents up to the smaller size. It may move the block, so the old pointer becomes invalid. On failure it returns NULL and leaves the original block untouched, so never write `p = realloc(p, n)` directly (you would leak p).

sections.heading: free
sections.body: `free(p)` returns a block obtained from malloc, calloc, or realloc. `free(NULL)` is a safe no-op. Freeing twice or freeing a pointer that did not come from the allocator is undefined behavior. Set the pointer to NULL afterward.

sections.heading: A growable array
sections.body: Doubling capacity when full gives amortized O(1) appends.

bullets: One block of rows*cols ints, index as m[i*cols + j]: best locality and a single free.
Array of row pointers, each malloc'd: flexible rows, many frees.
Pointer to array: `int (*m)[cols] = malloc(rows * sizeof *m);` gives m[i][j] syntax with one block.
Memory leak: lost pointer, missing free.
Use after free and double free.
Buffer overrun: writing past the requested size.
Wrong size such as `malloc(sizeof p)` for a pointer p (gives the pointer size).
Casting malloc's result in C (unnecessary; can hide a missing #include <stdlib.h>).

sections.body: The allocator stores a small header before each block with its size, and keeps free blocks in bins or lists. glibc's ptmalloc uses arenas, and large requests use mmap. Metadata next to your data is why heap overflows are dangerous.

malloc returns memory aligned for any standard type. `aligned_alloc(alignment, size)` (C11) or `posix_memalign` provide stricter alignment (SIMD, page-aligned I/O). `alloca` allocates on the stack and is non-standard and risky.
Compile with `-fsanitize=address -g` to catch overflows, use-after-free, and leaks; run under Valgrind for similar reports; `mtrace` and `MALLOC_CHECK_` are lightweight glibc aids.

takeaways: malloc: uninitialized; calloc: zeroed and overflow-safe; realloc: may move; free: once only.
Always check for NULL, and assign realloc to a temporary.
Use sizeof *p, set pointers to NULL after free.
